public_rationale: The contemporaneous programming study found both correct and incorrect answers and observed users missing errors in convincing responses. The January legal study independently found frequent errors and unreliable model self-assessment. Together they support Marcus's ordinary claim that plausible answers could be false and that users could struggle to tell which to trust.
limitations: The direct user study was small and concerned programming.
Legal error rates apply to the tested questions and models, not all chatbot use.
The claim does not establish that every user or every task faces the same difficulty.

evidence.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Users get tricked by appearance.'
evidence.explanation: The study assessed 517 programming answers and reported 52% incorrect, demonstrating mixed accuracy. Its 12-participant user study found that plausible presentation could obscure errors, directly supporting the user-detection component.

The January report documents frequent factual errors in legal queries and unreliable model self-assessment. It supports the absence of a dependable confidence signal, although it does not directly measure end-user detection.
